title: [Chapitre] IV. Analysis situs (première mouture) : notes manuscrites (10/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from pp. 80–84): a set 𝓕 of 'figures' carries two order relations. ≤ is presumably inclusion-like, and ≼ is a second, finer kind of inclusion. A guess is that ≤ means 'closed in' and ≼ means 'open in', or the reverse. M ⊂ 𝓕 is a distinguished subclass. The composite relation is defined by F ≪ G ⇔ ∃G' with F ≤ G' ≼ G, i.e. an ≤-sub-object of a ≼-sub-object, analogous to 'locally closed = closed in an open'. Page 82 asks whether ≪ is an order and, for antisymmetry, states a corollary of axiom C8: if F ≪ G and G ≪ F then F = G.

This page proves that corollary.
- F ≪ G gives F ≤ G' ≼ G, and G ≪ F gives G ≤ F' ≼ F.
- Axiom C7 is an exchange or completion axiom: a ≼ followed by a ≤ can be rewritten as a ≤ followed by a ≼. Applied to G' ≼ G ≤ F', it produces H with G' ≤ H ≼ F'. This is the same as axiom a) on p. 84.
- By transitivity, F ≤ G' ≤ H and H ≼ F' ≼ F. Hence (*) F ≤ H ≼ F.
- Axiom C8(a) (if X ≤ Φ ≼ X then X = Φ) gives F = H.
- Then F ≤ G' ≤ H = F gives G' = F, and F = H ≼ F' ≼ F gives F' = F (antisymmetry of ≼).
- Hence (**) F ≼ G ≤ F. Axiom C8(b) (if X ≼ Ψ ≤ X then X = Ψ) gives F = G.

Next, Grothendieck starts proving a first point via F ≤ G, unpacked as: for all X ∈ M, X ≤ F ⇒ X ≤ G. He refers to a condition on p. 80.

The closing lines are hard to read. They seem to comment that he tried to detail the argument as fully as possible, without relying on diagram-style reasoning, thanks to C5.

A vertical marginal note seems to say that (*) is not what one actually has at that point, and that one should use (**)-type relations; it involves H ≤ F and H ≼ H. This is presumably a self-correction of how the M-elementwise version of C8 is applied.

Page 84 then abstracts all this into an order-theoretic remark: two orders on a set with axioms a) (unique completion), b) (non-unique completion) and c) (F ≤ G ≼ F ⇒ F = G). Then ≪ is an order relation.

Purpose: to set up, in the 1986 'Analysis situs' tame-topology framework, a well-behaved order 'locally-closed-type inclusion' generated by two primitive inclusion relations.
errors: The argument is correct given C7 in the form 'G' ≼ G ≤ F' ⇒ ∃H, G' ≤ H ≼ F'' and C8(a),(b) as stated on p. 82. It also uses antisymmetry of both ≤ and ≼ implicitly.

C8 on p. 82 is formulated for X ∈ M, whereas here it is applied to arbitrary F ∈ 𝓕. That is a gap unless C8 holds for all of 𝓕, as in axiom c) of p. 84. The marginal note seems to flag exactly this ('Mais ce n'est pas (*)...'), and p. 84 restates c) for general elements.

ideas.what: Composite of two order relations (G ≤ F' ≼ F) is again an order, given an exchange/completion axiom and a 'no loops' axiom F ≤ G ≼ F ⇒ F = G
ideas.modern_name: Composition of relations / distributive-law-style commutation of two partial orders; the order-theoretic shadow of factorization systems (e.g. locally closed = closed∘open)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore order theory; Beck (distributive laws, 1969) and Freyd–Kelly (factorization systems, 1972) for categorical analogues
ideas.where_published: Not in published texts as far as I know; the 'locally closed' notion is standard (EGA 0/I)

ideas.what: Antisymmetry of ≪ via the completion axiom C7 and cancellation axioms C8(a),(b)

deep.surprise_reason: A careful but routine order-theoretic verification (antisymmetry of a composite order) inside the 1986 tame-topology notes. It is interesting only as a glimpse of Grothendieck axiomatizing 'locally closed' inclusion via two primitive orders; there is no new mathematics here.
transcription_corrections: The vertical relation under G in both diagrams is G ≤ F' (G above F'), not a generic '∨|'. Likewise G' ≤ H in the second diagram (written with a doubled symbol).

The last paragraph probably reads something like 'On a essayé ici de détailler aussi bien que possible, sans écrire de raisonnements en diagrammes(?), grâce à C5'; the machine reading 'employé ... de ne' is doubtful.
'Prouvons d'abord ce premier pt : il suffit de prouver F ≤ G, i.e. ∀ X ∈ M, X ≤ F ⇒ X ≤ G, c'est là ... la condition p. 80' — the '∀' is written as a symbol, not 'si'.
The marginal note is largely illegible; it plausibly reads 'Mais ce n'est pas (*) qu'on a en fait, mais ... d'où ... H ≤ F ... H ≼ H'.
